summary: Defines the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules, giving common data types such as shared formats a name. It is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1903.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shared set of ready-made data types so MIB writers don't have to reinvent them every time.

questions: what is a textual convention in snmp
how are snmp table rows created
subtitle: A way to give MIB data types their own names, meanings and display formats, plus the first set of ready-made ones.

tldr.problem: MIB designers often need types that are like the SMI base types but with a different name and more precise meaning, such as a MAC address or a boolean.
tldr.mechanism: The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro names a new type, gives its syntax, status, description and an optional display hint, and the RFC defines an initial set including DisplayString, MacAddress, TruthValue, RowStatus, TimeStamp and DateAndTime.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 58) that obsoletes RFC 1903. Objects using a textual convention are still encoded by the rules of their underlying primitive type.

today: RFC 2579 is an Internet Standard (STD 58) published in April 1999 and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 1903 and is a companion to RFC 2578.

sections.title: Why Textual Conventions Exist
sections.content:
MIB modules are written in the adapted ASN.1 subset called the Structure of Management Information, defined in RFC 2578. When designing a module it is often useful to define new types similar to the SMI types: a different name, a similar syntax, but a more precise meaning. These are textual conventions, used for the convenience of humans reading the MIB module.

Objects defined with a textual convention are always encoded by the rules of their primitive type, so nothing changes on the wire. The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro conveys the syntax and semantics, and this document defines the initial set available to all MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: A textual convention is a nickname for a kind of answer, like writing yes or no instead of 1 or 2. It makes the form easier for people to read.

sections.title: The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION Macro
sections.content:
The macro has an optional DISPLAY-HINT, a required STATUS (current, deprecated or obsolete), a required DESCRIPTION, an optional REFERENCE and a required SYNTAX. The syntax must be a base type or the BITS construct, so a textual convention cannot refer to another textual convention.

A convention's name uses letters and digits, starts with an upper-case letter, must not clash with the reserved words of RFC 2578, should not be all upper case and must not exceed 64 characters (over 32 is not recommended). Names used in all standard information modules must be unique, and hyphens are not allowed except in modules converted from SMIv1. The syntax may be sub-typed the same way as in an OBJECT-TYPE clause.
sections.plainLanguage: To make a new label you give it a name, say what it means and say what kind of answer it holds underneath.

sections.title: The Initial Set of Conventions
sections.content:
Text and addresses. DisplayString is NVT ASCII text (character codes 0-127) with the special meanings of RFC 854, at most 255 characters, and a display hint of 255a. PhysAddress is a media- or physical-level address, and MacAddress is an 802 MAC address of exactly 6 octets in the canonical order of IEEE 802.1a. TDomain denotes a kind of transport service, and TAddress is a transport address of 1 to 255 octets that is always read in the context of a TDomain.

Values and identifiers. TruthValue is an integer with true(1) and false(2). TestAndIncr supports atomic operations: a set succeeds only if the supplied value exactly matches the current one, and then the value is incremented, wrapping to zero after 2147483647. AutonomousType is an independently extensible type identification OBJECT IDENTIFIER. VariablePointer points to a specific object instance such as sysContact.0, and RowPointer points to a conceptual row. The older InstancePointer is marked obsolete and replaced by those two.

Time and storage. TimeStamp holds the value of sysUpTime when something happened, and the text notes that after approximately 497 days without re-initialization it wraps around, which can cause ambiguity. TimeInterval is a period in units of 0.01 seconds. DateAndTime is an 8 or 11 octet value covering year, month, day, hour, minutes, seconds, deci-seconds and an optional offset from UTC. StorageType describes how a row is kept: other(1), volatile(2), nonVolatile(3), permanent(4) or readOnly(5).
sections.plainLanguage: The starter box has labels for text, hardware addresses, yes or no, dates and times, and how long a row of information should be remembered.

sections.title: RowStatus: Creating and Deleting Rows
sections.content:
RowStatus manages how table rows are created and deleted, and is the syntax of a row's status column. It has six values. active(1) and notInService(2) may be read or written, notReady(3) may only be read, and createAndGo(4), createAndWait(5) and destroy(6) are actions that may be written but never read. Reading a row's status therefore returns only notReady, notInService or active.

The RFC walks through four interactions for creating a row: choosing an unused instance identifier, creating the row, initializing columns that have no default, and making the row available. A station can create and activate in one set with createAndGo, which fails with inconsistentValue if the agent lacks enough information. Or it can use createAndWait, fill in the missing columns step by step, and finally set the status to active. An agent that does not support createAndWait answers wrongValue.

If a station never finishes, the row would sit in notInService or notReady forever. The agent must detect rows left that way for an abnormally long time and remove them. Unless the status column's DESCRIPTION says otherwise, the suggested period is approximately 5 minutes. Setting destroy deletes all instances of the row, whatever its current state.
sections.plainLanguage: Making a new row is like setting a table at a restaurant: you reserve it first, fill in the details, then say it is ready. If you never show up, the staff clear it away after a while.

sections.title: Display Hints
sections.content:
A DISPLAY-HINT suggests how to show a value. It must not be present for conventions based on OBJECT IDENTIFIER, IpAddress, Counter32, Counter64 or any enumerated syntax.

For integers the hint is a format character: x hexadecimal, d decimal, o octal or b binary. For d it can be followed by a hyphen and a number giving the implied decimal point, so d-2 renders a value of 1234 as 12.34.

For octet strings the hint is a list of specifications of five parts: an optional repeat indicator (an asterisk), an octet length, a display format (x, d, o, a for ASCII or t for UTF-8), an optional separator character and an optional repeat terminator. For example MacAddress uses 1x:, meaning each octet is shown in hexadecimal followed by a colon. If octets remain after the last specification, it is applied again until none are left.
sections.plainLanguage: A display hint is a note saying how to print a value, like putting a decimal point in the right place or writing a hardware address as pairs of digits with colons between.

sections.title: Revising a Convention
sections.content:
A textual convention may be revised only if the change cannot cause interoperability problems over the wire between old and new implementations. Anything else requires a new convention with a new name.

Allowed revisions are: adding enumerations or changing labels, moving current to deprecated or obsolete (or deprecated to obsolete) with an updated description, adding or updating REFERENCE, adding or updating the display hint, clarifying the description, and any editorial change. Because the macro now exists, a definition such as DisplayString ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (0..255)) should be replaced by a TEXTUAL-CONVENTION.
sections.plainLanguage: You can fix the wording on a label, but if you change what it means you have to make a new label with a new name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines a way to define new data types for the language used to write and read descriptions of management information. It states that these data types have no security impact on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: These are only labels for writing things down, so they do not add any security risk.

viz.caption: SIMPLIFIED ROWSTATUS LIFE CYCLE (ROW CREATION AND DELETION)

items.label: active
items.desc: Row is available for use by the managed device. Readable and writable.

items.label: notInService
items.desc: Row exists but is unavailable. Readable and writable.

items.label: notReady
items.desc: Row exists but required information is missing. Read only.

items.label: createAndGo
items.desc: Create a row and make it active. Write only.

items.label: createAndWait
items.desc: Create a row without making it available. Write only.

items.label: destroy
items.desc: Delete all instances of the row. Write only.
